stories.title: Nvidia Loses Its Architect at the Worst Possible Moment
stories.story:
For thirty-three years, Jensen Huang was not merely Nvidia's CEO — he was its product vision, its diplomatic face in Beijing, and its most credible voice to Wall Street. That era ended abruptly on November 12 when Nvidia announced his immediate resignation, two days after the New York Times reported he had carried on an affair with a businesswoman U.S. intelligence believed to be a Chinese agent, and a separate affair with an Nvidia vice president who reported directly to him.

The personal scandal metastasized into a structural one. Nvidia's board had initially said Huang would stay during an internal investigation into whether he had been 'the target of a foreign intelligence effort.' Then a second affair surfaced, Washington officials called for his congressional testimony, and within hours he was gone. CFO Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.

The ripple effects reach well beyond one company. Nvidia participated in roughly 105 startup funding rounds this year — often as the largest check in the room — effectively acting as the central bank of the AI ecosystem. Founders and venture capitalists are now repricing deals on the assumption that the 'Nvidia put' is over: that anchor capital disappears when its author does. Shares fell nearly 8% on the news.

The deeper implication is geopolitical. Huang had personally championed Nvidia's access to the Chinese market and navigated successive rounds of U.S. chip export controls with unusual agility. His successor will inherit both the best-positioned semiconductor franchise on earth and a congressional spotlight that his predecessor's scandal has made far brighter. The question now is whether Nvidia's moat is durable enough to outlast the man who dug it.
stories.hook: It turns out the most important chip in AI wasn't silicon — it was the person who convinced everyone to trust the company making it.
stories.source: Al Jazeera, ABC News, NBC News, PBS NewsHour — November 12–14, 2026

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO Is the AI Sector's First Real Reckoning
stories.story:
For five years, the AI industry has operated as a kind of faith-based economy — valuations soaring on projections, capital flowing between companies that largely sell to each other, and no public market forcing honest price discovery. That changes next week. Anthropic, maker of the Claude model family, is set to price its IPO on November 18 at between $70 and $78 per share, targeting a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion and raising up to $90.4 billion — a figure that would surpass SpaceX's June listing and become the largest public offering in history.

The mechanics are revealing. The raise is not a single clean equity sale. It bundles 825 million Class A public shares with a $26 billion private placement purchased by backers including Nvidia and Microsoft — the same companies that depend on Anthropic's compute purchases to justify their own AI revenue lines. The circularity is deliberate and fragile: Anthropic simultaneously committed to spending $30 billion on Microsoft Azure infrastructure running on Nvidia chips. These are not arm's-length transactions. They are a supply chain masquerading as a capital structure.

What makes this consequential today, beyond the record size, is timing. With Jensen Huang's departure having already rattled the AI ecosystem and Nvidia's role as the sector's de facto venture backstop suddenly in doubt, the Anthropic IPO becomes the first clean public signal of whether institutional investors, not venture insiders, actually believe the AI demand story. The book is reportedly oversubscribed and bankers are now weighing pricing above the stated range. Goldman Sachs projects Anthropic's revenue could reach $685 billion by 2030. The company lost $42 billion in 2025. The public market will now have to reconcile both numbers.
stories.hook: The largest IPO in history is also the first time anyone outside the AI inner circle gets to vote on whether any of this actually makes sense.

stories.title: The SEC Stopped Policing Public Companies. The Numbers Are Stark.
stories.story:
For most of its modern history, the Securities and Exchange Commission operated on a simple theory of deterrence: visible punishment changes behavior at scale. If a company knows it will be caught and fined, it will think twice before misstating earnings, burying a conflict of interest, or bribing a foreign official. That theory is now being tested in its inverse.

In fiscal year 2026, the SEC brought just 16 enforcement actions against public companies and their subsidiaries — a 71% drop from the prior year and the lowest figure ever recorded since systematic tracking began in 2010. Total monetary settlements against public companies fell to $184 million, more than $600 million below the year before. For the first time in the database's history, not a single action involved Foreign Corrupt Practices Act allegations. The SEC's overall caseload — 348 actions of all types — was the lightest since 1991.

The causes are layered but not mysterious. Chair Paul Atkins arrived with an explicit mandate to end what his predecessor called 'regulation by enforcement.' A 43-day government shutdown early in the fiscal year disrupted the enforcement pipeline. Staff cuts removed roughly 20% of SEC personnel, including 13% of enforcement division headcount at headquarters. The machine slowed because it was designed to slow.

What this implies forward is the harder question. Deterrence theory says corporate misconduct is a probabilistic calculation: expected penalty times probability of enforcement. When the probability collapses, the calculus changes — not overnight, not uniformly, but structurally. The bond market is already repricing AI-sector financing risk; the SEC's retreat means less visibility into the numbers underpinning those bets. The next fraud cycle, when it arrives, will have had years to compound in the dark.
stories.hook: When the cop leaves the beat, it doesn't mean nothing happens — it means you hear about it later.
stories.source: InvestmentNews / Cornerstone Research SEED Database, November 2026
